newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: BIL asset sale may be imminent - analysts.
newsitem.headline: BIL asset sale may be imminent - analysts.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd (BIL) may be about to sell one of its assets, possibly Australia's Weeks Bass Strait Royalty, share analysts said on Thursday.

The New Zealand Herald newspaper said a sale by BIL of Weeks for around NZ$350 million was on the cards but analysts were not sure the matter was so clear-cut. The consensus among them was that Weeks was just one of four or five distinct possibilities.
A spokesman for the diversified investment company declined to comment on the talk.
The Herald report said the sale of the Weeks' oil royalty before BIL's June year balance date would make up a shortfall in covering its dividend payout and interest on convertible notes.
It would also assist BIL in meeting market forecasts for an annual profit of around NZ$300 million for the June year.
But analysts said they felt BIL had sufficient resources to cover its commitments to both share and note holders.
Furthermore, BIL was relatively unfazed about meeting forecasts, especially since many parts of the BIL stable were performing strongly relative to the company's cost of entry.
"The market is expecting an asset sale transaction. Whether something happens with Weeks remains to be seen," Robert Bode, head of research at Merill Lynch, he said.
"Generally there is a feeling in the market that something will transpire in the not too distant future," he said.
The Weeks investment had been lucrative for BIL and is held via its Australian Consolidated Investments Ltd unit.
BIL receives a 1.38 percent direct royalty from the Bass Strait well. This contributed NZ$36 million in 1996.
"It really depends on value. If someone is prepared to pay them a full price, then yes, they could well decide that it's a mature investment and to divert funds elsewhere," Bode added.
But Bode said Weeks was "not at the forefront of people's expectations" because it was a strong cash contributor.
Guy Hallwright at First NZ Capital said that, while Weeks had been a stronger performer, it didn't quite fit the BIL modus operandi of adding value to its investments.

"I'm sure it's a great investment to have but so is putting money in the bank -- the money just rolls in. It doesn't seem to me to be a very efficient use of an investment company's capital," Hallwright said.
Weeks appeared a reasonable guess, but another possibility might be the BIL's Broadway property assets in Edinburgh following their separation from BIL's Thistle Hotels.
Kevin Bennett at Doyle Paterson Brown said a Weeks sale was one of a raft of possibilities but that BIL was now showing less of a tendency to aim for profit targets just for the sake of it.

That perception had been supported by how well its general portfolio was performing. Among those investments were Coles Myer (7.7 percent-owned), James Hardie Industries (28 percent) and Fairfax (20 percent).

"You could say that their investment philosophy seems to be working quite well at the moment. So given that positive appreciation going on in quite a bit of their portfolio, it takes the pressure off (needing) to report earnings of X percent," Bennett said.

Furthermore, 46-percent owned Thistle appeared to be progressing. The company this week reported a 13 percent rise in turnover in the first 16 weeks of the current year, and supported a solid rise in the company's shares on Wednesday.
The shares rose again on Thursday, closing up 2 cents at NZ1.36 on volume of about four million shares.
--Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
